Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- Canadian ski resort gondola cars that were left dangling and swaying with terrified skiers inside failed because ice buildup snapped a supporting tower, the resort said Thursday. One gondola car is suspended above an icy creek at a ski resort near Whistler, British Columbia. In a rare occurrence called ice-jacking, water seeped into the lower section of the lift tower and turned to ice Tuesday at Whistler Blackcomb resort, 177 kilometers (110 miles) north of Vancouver, a resort official said in a press release Thursday. The lift hangs from a tower that is spliced into two parts. Extremely cold temperatures caused the ice buildup that exerted 800 tons of pressure between the two parts that hold the tower together, causing them to rupture, according to Whistler Blackcomb. The section of the lift affected by the accident had 15 cars going up the mountain and 15 coming down at the time, but they weren't carrying a lot of passengers, according to Doug Forseth, senior vice president of the resort. He said 53 passengers had been rescued from the stranded cars. No skiers at the Whistler, British Columbia, resort were seriously injured. "The towers are not normally designed to allow for any water penetration and so this failure is a very unusual situation," said Warren Sparks, senior vice president of Doppelmayr Canada, the engineering firm that investigated the accident. They are trying to figure out what caused the water to pool. He said independent structural engineers are examining the tower from Vancouver-based CVMM Consulting Engineers. "The evidence so far indicates a sudden rupture rather than a fatigue failure over an extended period," Sparks said. At least two gondola cars broke away and hit the ground, both from relatively low heights near the tower that split, and caused the system's heavy cable line to slacken, according to Tyler Noble, a reporter for CNNRadio affiliate CKNW in Vancouver. "One hit a bus stop and the other hit a house," Noble said Wednesday. "Another one was suspended over a creek, but everyone is out of that car." The broken Excaliber Gondola was not operating Thursday. Whistler engineers checked eight similar towers across the two mountains of the resort. All passed those inspections, and are open Thursday, the release said. The British Columbia Authority says it does not expect to rescind operating permits on any lifts at the resort, other than the Excaliber Gondola. Jeff Colburn, general manager of Silver Mountain Resort in Kellogg, Idaho, said a lift tower at his resort was similarly damaged by ice in December 2006. The damage was discovered in the morning before the slopes opened, so no one was endangered, he said. The damaged tower was replaced in about three weeks, Colburn said, and the resort's business was not significantly disrupted. "We check our towers in the summer now, and we also check before we open up for ski season as well just to make sure they don't have any water in them, and we've worked with the manufacturers," he said. Holes have been drilled in the bases of towers so that water can drain out, Colburn said. CNN's Ashley Fantz and Jim Kavanagh contributed to this report.

(CNN) -- Gondola cars at a Canadian ski resort left dangling and swaying with terrified skiers aboard failed after ice buildup caused a supporting tower to snap, resort officials announced Thursday. One gondola car remains suspended above an icy creek at the resort near Whistler, British Columbia.

In a rare phenomenon known as ice-jacking, water seeped into the lower section of the lift tower and froze on Tuesday at Whistler Blackcomb resort, located 177 kilometers (110 miles) north of Vancouver, a resort official explained in a press release issued Thursday. The lift is suspended from a tower constructed in two spliced sections. Extremely cold temperatures caused ice to accumulate, exerting roughly 800 tons of pressure on the joint connecting the two sections and ultimately causing them to rupture, according to Whistler Blackcomb.

At the time of the incident, the affected section of the lift was carrying 15 cars ascending and 15 descending the mountain, though passenger loads were relatively light, said Doug Forseth, the resort's senior vice president. He confirmed that 53 passengers had been safely rescued from the stranded cars, and no skiers at the Whistler resort sustained serious injuries.

"The towers are not normally designed to allow for any water penetration, so this failure represents a highly unusual situation," said Warren Sparks, senior vice president of Doppelmayr Canada, the engineering firm investigating the incident. Engineers are still working to determine the source of the water accumulation. Sparks noted that independent structural engineers from Vancouver-based CVMM Consulting Engineers are examining the tower. "The evidence so far points to a sudden rupture rather than fatigue failure developing over an extended period," he said.

According to Tyler Noble, a reporter for CNN Radio affiliate CKNW in Vancouver, at least two gondola cars broke free and struck the ground—both falling from relatively low heights near the point where the tower split, which caused the system's heavy cable line to go slack. "One hit a bus stop, and the other hit a house," Noble reported Wednesday. "Another was left suspended over a creek, but everyone has since been evacuated from that car."

The damaged Excalibur Gondola remained out of service Thursday. Meanwhile, Whistler engineers inspected eight comparable towers across the resort's two mountains; all passed inspection and were operational Thursday, according to the press release. The British Columbia Authority stated it does not anticipate revoking operating permits for any of the resort's lifts other than the Excalibur Gondola.

Jeff Colburn, general manager of Silver Mountain Resort in Kellogg, Idaho, recalled a similar incident of ice-related tower damage at his own resort in December 2006. The damage was discovered that morning before the slopes opened, ensuring no one was put at risk, he said. The compromised tower was replaced within roughly three weeks, and the resort's operations were not significantly disrupted as a result.

"We now check our towers during the summer, and again before the start of ski season, just to make sure they haven't accumulated any water—we've also collaborated with the manufacturers on this," Colburn said. He added that drainage holes have since been drilled into the bases of the towers to prevent water from pooling.

CNN's Ashley Fantz and Jim Kavanagh contributed to this report.

# Ski Lift Malfunction at Canadian Resort Traced to Ice Damage

(CNN) -- A frightening incident at a British Columbia ski resort, where gondola cars were left hanging precariously with frightened passengers aboard, occurred because accumulated ice caused a support tower to break, resort officials announced Thursday.

At Whistler Blackcomb resort—located 177 kilometers (110 miles) north of Vancouver—one gondola remained stranded above a frozen creek following the mishap. According to a resort spokesperson, the incident stemmed from an unusual phenomenon known as ice-jacking: water had infiltrated the tower's lower portion on Tuesday and subsequently froze solid.

The lift system relies on a tower constructed in two connected segments. Bitter cold temperatures allowed ice to build up, generating roughly 800 tons of force between the joined sections and ultimately causing them to break apart, resort representatives explained.

At the moment of the failure, this particular lift section carried 15 cars traveling upward and another 15 descending, though passenger loads were relatively light, according to Doug Forseth, the resort's senior vice president. He confirmed that rescue teams successfully evacuated 53 passengers from the immobilized gondolas, and fortunately, none of the skiers sustained serious injuries.

Warren Sparks, senior vice president at Doppelmayr Canada—the firm investigating the incident—noted that towers typically aren't built to withstand water infiltration, making this failure highly unusual. Investigators are now working to determine how water accumulated in the structure in the first place. Sparks added that independent engineers from CVMM Consulting Engineers, based in Vancouver, are currently examining the damaged tower. "The evidence so far indicates a sudden rupture rather than a fatigue failure over an extended period," he stated.

CKNW radio reporter Tyler Noble (a CNN Radio affiliate in Vancouver) reported that a minimum of two gondola cars detached and fell to the ground, both dropping from relatively modest heights near the fractured tower, which caused the main cable to lose tension. "One hit a bus stop and the other hit a house," Noble reported Wednesday, adding, "Another one was suspended over a creek, but everyone is out of that car."

The affected Excalibur Gondola remained closed Thursday. Resort engineering staff subsequently examined eight comparable towers throughout the resort's two mountains—all passed inspection and reopened Thursday, according to the official statement. British Columbia's regulatory authority indicated it doesn't anticipate revoking operating licenses for any resort lifts besides the Excalibur Gondola.

A similar incident occurred at Silver Mountain Resort in Kellogg, Idaho, according to general manager Jeff Colburn, who recalled ice damage to one of their lift towers back in December 2006. That damage was caught during a morning inspection before slopes opened, meaning no visitors faced risk. The compromised tower took approximately three weeks to replace, Colburn noted, with minimal impact on the resort's operations overall.

"We check our towers in the summer now, and we also check before we open up for ski season as well just to make sure they don't have any water in them, and we've worked with the manufacturers," Colburn explained. He added that tower bases now have drilled holes allowing any accumulated water to drain away safely.

*CNN's Ashley Fantz and Jim Kavanagh contributed to this report.*

# Gondola Malfunction at Whistler Blackcomb Sends Skiers Plummeting, Prompts Investigation

**WHISTLER, British Columbia** — A gondola cabin at Whistler Blackcomb ski resort dropped several meters after a supporting tower was damaged by ice buildup, resort officials confirmed Tuesday, sending shockwaves through the popular winter destination during the height of ski season.

The incident occurred Monday afternoon on the Peak 2 Peak gondola line, which connects Whistler Mountain and Blackcomb Mountain, when a support structure gave way following what engineers described as significant ice accumulation on the tower's cabling and structural components.

Resort officials said the malfunction caused at least one gondola cabin to fall approximately 10 meters before emergency stabilization systems engaged, halting further descent. Several passengers aboard the cabin sustained injuries, though none were reported as life-threatening.

"We are grateful that our safety systems prevented what could have been a far more serious incident," said Whistler Blackcomb spokesperson Marcus Chen in a statement released Tuesday morning. "The safety of our guests and staff remains our absolute top priority."

Emergency responders were dispatched to the scene within minutes, according to local authorities. The Whistler Fire Department and mountain rescue teams worked to evacuate passengers from the affected gondola line, a process that took several hours due to the complexity of the terrain and weather conditions.

Four passengers were transported to Whistler Health Care Centre for treatment of injuries including lacerations and suspected fractures. Two individuals were later transferred to Vancouver General Hospital for further evaluation, though their conditions have been described as stable.

The Peak 2 Peak gondola, one of the longest continuous lifts of its kind in the world, has been suspended indefinitely while engineers conduct a full inspection of all support towers along the route. The British Columbia Safety Authority, which oversees mechanical safety standards in the province, has launched an investigation into the incident.

Preliminary findings suggest that unusually heavy ice formation on the tower—exacerbated by a recent freeze-thaw cycle in the region—compromised structural integrity at the point of failure. Whistler has experienced volatile weather patterns this winter, with temperatures fluctuating dramatically between daytime highs above freezing and overnight lows well below.

"Ice loading on mountain infrastructure is something we monitor constantly, but this appears to have been an extreme and unusual event," said structural engineer Diane Whitfield, who is not affiliated with the resort but has consulted on similar cases. "These systems are built with significant safety margins, but Mother Nature can still surprise us."

This is not the first time weather-related issues have affected lift operations at the resort. Whistler Blackcomb has faced scrutiny in recent years over aging infrastructure and the challenges of maintaining equipment in increasingly unpredictable mountain climates.

Skiers and snowboarders at the resort expressed shock and concern following the incident.

"We were in line for that exact gondola about twenty minutes before it happened," said tourist Sarah Jennings, who was visiting from Seattle. "It's terrifying to think about how close that could have been us."

Local business owners worry about the economic impact of an extended closure, as the Peak 2 Peak gondola serves as a critical link between the resort's two mountains during peak tourist season.

Whistler Blackcomb has not provided a timeline for when the gondola line might reopen, stating only that safety inspections "will take as long as necessary" before operations resume. The Transportation Safety Board of Canada has not indicated whether it will join the provincial investigation, though sources familiar with the matter say federal officials are monitoring the situation closely.

# Skiers Stranded for Hours After Gondola Tower Failure Sparks Emergency Rescue

**MOUNTAIN VALLEY** — Dozens of skiers and snowboarders were left dangling hundreds of feet above the slopes for several hours Saturday after a support tower malfunction brought a popular gondola line to an abrupt halt, triggering a complex rescue operation involving ski patrol, fire crews, and specialized high-angle rescue teams.

## The Incident

The gondola, which carries visitors from the base area to the upper mountain lodge, stopped suddenly at approximately 11:15 a.m. local time when what resort officials described as a "mechanical fault" occurred at one of the line's support towers. Approximately 30 gondola cars, carrying an estimated 120 passengers, were suspended along the cable line when the system automatically shut down.

"We heard a loud grinding noise, and then everything just stopped," said Marcus Chen, a skier from out of state who was riding in one of the stranded cars. "At first we thought it was just a brief pause, but after twenty minutes without movement, people started getting nervous."

Resort spokesperson Elena Ramirez confirmed that an automatic safety system detected an anomaly in the tower's mechanism and halted the lift as a precautionary measure. "Our systems are designed to stop immediately at the first sign of irregularity," Ramirez said. "While this resulted in passengers being stranded longer than anyone would like, the safety protocols functioned exactly as intended."

## Rescue Efforts

Resort officials activated their emergency response plan within minutes, coordinating with local fire departments and mountain rescue specialists. Rescue teams used a combination of methods to reach stranded passengers, including rope-access techniques for cars closest to towers and, in some cases, ski patrol members skiing beneath cars to communicate with passengers and pass up blankets, water, and hand warmers.

For cars situated over cliffside terrain or steep drops, rescuers relied on a secondary evacuation cable system, lowering passengers individually in rescue harnesses to waiting snowmobiles below.

"This was a slow, methodical process because safety had to come first," said county fire captain David Whitfield, whose crew assisted in the operation. "You're dealing with cold temperatures, high winds, and passengers who may not have any experience with rope work. Every evacuation had to be done carefully."

By 4:30 p.m., resort officials confirmed that all passengers had been safely evacuated. Several individuals were treated for mild hypothermia and exposure, though no serious injuries were reported. Two passengers were transported to a local hospital as a precaution.

## Passenger Accounts

Passengers described a mix of anxiety and camaraderie during the hours-long wait. Temperatures hovered in the low 20s Fahrenheit, and gusting winds caused some cars to sway noticeably.

"We tried to stay calm and keep each other's spirits up," said Angela Torres, who was riding with her two teenage children. "The resort staff below kept shouting updates to us, which helped. But I won't lie—it was terrifying at first."

Some passengers reported using emergency blankets provided in gondola cars, while others said they wrapped themselves in extra layers of clothing intended for the slopes.

## Safety Inspections and Investigation

State transportation safety officials, who oversee aerial lift operations, announced that the gondola line would remain closed pending a full inspection. Investigators from the state's tramway safety board arrived on-site Saturday evening to begin examining the tower mechanism and cable system.

"Our inspectors will conduct a thorough review of the mechanical components, electrical systems, and structural integrity of the tower in question," said board director Patricia Nguyen. "We want to understand precisely what caused the malfunction before any decision is made about reopening."

Resort officials stated that the gondola had passed its most recent state-mandated inspection earlier in the ski season and that maintenance records showed no prior issues with the affected tower. Nevertheless, management said they would voluntarily keep the lift closed until investigators complete their assessment, and that additional lifts using similar mechanical components would undergo expedited safety checks as a precaution.

Industry experts noted that while gondola malfunctions are rare, resorts nationwide have increased scrutiny of aging lift infrastructure following a handful of high-profile incidents in recent years.

"Aerial lifts are engineered with multiple redundant safety systems," said Robert Kessler, a mechanical engineer specializing in ropeway transport. "When something like this happens, it usually indicates a component failure was caught early by the safety system—which, while inconvenient for passengers, is the system working as designed rather than failing."

## Moving Forward

The resort has offered full refunds to all guests affected by the closure and issued season pass credits to those directly involved in the incident. Grief and stress counselors were made available on-site for passengers who requested support following the ordeal.

Officials say they expect to receive preliminary findings from the safety inspection within the coming days, though a full report could take several weeks. The resort's other lifts continued normal operations throughout the weekend.

"Our priority now is understanding exactly what happened and ensuring it doesn't happen again," Ramirez said. "The safety of our guests is not something we take lightly."

*This is a developing story and will be updated as more information becomes available.*
